questions.question: Give one utilitarian and one ethical argument for conserving biodiversity.
questions.solution: Utilitarian: species provide ecosystem services and resources — pollination, medicines (many drugs come from plants), water purification — whose loss costs the economy directly. Ethical: every species has intrinsic value and a right to exist, independent of its use to humans; we hold it in trust for future generations. Both arguments lead to the same action.

questions.question: What distinguishes 'endangered' from 'vulnerable' in the IUCN Red List, and why does the classification matter?
questions.solution: Both measure extinction risk, but with different thresholds: endangered = very high risk (e.g. >50% probability of extinction in 10 years/3 generations); vulnerable = high risk (weaker thresholds, e.g. 20% in 20 years). The category sets the legal protection level and conservation priority — resources flow to the most threatened first.

questions.question: Why is a national park generally better than a zoo for conservation, and when is a zoo the only option?
questions.solution: In-situ (national parks, reserves) preserves the species WITH its ecosystem — prey, pollinators, evolutionary pressures intact, at population scale and lower cost per individual. Ex-situ (zoo, seed bank, tissue culture) preserves individuals outside the habitat — the last resort when the habitat is gone or the wild population is too small to be viable. Habitat conservation is the default; captivity is the backup.

questions.question: How did Nepal's tiger and rhino populations recover while many countries' declined?
questions.solution: Protected-area network expansion (national parks, reserves covering ~25% of the country), strict anti-poaching patrols with army support, and COMMUNITY participation — buffer-zone communities receive tourism revenue and user rights, giving locals a stake in protection. Law enforcement + benefit-sharing is the model that reversed the decline.

questions.question: Why do conservationists campaign around tigers and pandas rather than insects — and what is the strategy's weakness?
questions.solution: Charismatic flagships raise funds and public support far more effectively; protecting their large habitats incidentally protects thousands of co-occurring species (umbrella effect). Weakness: species outside the flagship's habitat, or uncharismatic ones (fungi, invertebrates), get little protection — the strategy is a means, not the goal.

questions.concept: Why small populations go extinct faster
questions.question: Two populations occupy equal habitat but one has 20 individuals and the other 2000. Why is the small one far likelier to vanish?
questions.solution: Small populations face genetic drift, inbreeding depression, Allee effects and random demographic/environmental fluctuation all at once — each of which small numbers amplify. Losing a few individuals can remove the last breeding pair. Extinction risk scales inversely with population size, so minimum viable population is a real management target, not a formality.

questions.concept: Why protected areas alone are insufficient
questions.question: A national park is strictly protected yet its wildlife still declines. Give reasons why legal boundaries fail to conserve.
questions.solution: Protected areas are often too small for wide-ranging animals, allow edge effects and human–wildlife conflict, and experience poaching and resource extraction inside. Species also need corridors to other areas to maintain gene flow. Conservation therefore needs landscape-level planning, community participation and enforcement, not just a line on a map. A boundary is a legal fact; ecology ignores it.

questions.question: Why does losing a species matter even if it has no obvious direct use?
questions.solution: Each species is a functional part of its ecosystem, contributing to pollination, nutrient cycling, pest control or food-web stability; its loss can destabilise the system that delivers services humans rely on. It also forecloses future uses — medicines, crop genes. Option value and ecosystem function both argue against treating species as individually expendable.
